title: Running Your First Python Program

items.title: The Hello World Tradition
items.content:
Since the 1970s, the universal first step in learning any new programming language is to make the computer print: `Hello, World!`.

In Python, doing this takes just one single, beautiful line of code:
```python
print("Hello, World!")
```
items.explanation: Since the 1970s, the universal first step in learning any new programming language is to make the computer print: `Hello, World!`. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt:
What does the following Python statement do?
```python
print("Hello, World!")
```
options: A. Sends the text to a physical paper printer in your office.
B. Displays the text 'Hello, World!' onto your console/screen.
C. Saves a new file named Hello.txt onto your hard drive.
D. Translates the words into machine code without displaying anything.
items.explanation: In programming, 'printing' historically meant sending text to a teletype or terminal screen. Today, `print()` outputs text to your computer's terminal or console output.

items.title: Two Ways to Run Python
items.content:
You can run Python code in two primary modes:

1. **Interactive Mode (REPL)**: Typing commands one line at a time into the Python prompt (`>>>`). Great for quick testing, but your code vanishes when you close the window.
2. **Script Mode**: Saving your code in a text file ending in `.py` and running it through Python. This permanently saves your program so it can be executed again and again.

items.explanation: Interactive mode provides an immediate Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL), while script mode reads and executes a saved file.

items.title: The .py File Extension
items.content:
Python source code files must be saved with the `.py` extension (for example, `main.py` or `hello.py`).

While a `.py` file is plain text, the extension signals to your operating system, your code editor, and the Python interpreter that the file contains Python instructions.

items.title: Running a Script from the Terminal
items.content:
To execute a script named `hello.py` from your terminal or command prompt, you type:
```bash
python hello.py
```
(On some macOS and Linux systems, you may type `python3 hello.py`).

Here, `python` is the program (the CPython interpreter) and `hello.py` is the file argument you are telling it to read and run.
items.explanation: To execute a script named `hello. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt:
A beginner opens their terminal, types `python` to enter the interactive prompt (`>>>`), and then tries to type:
`>>> python hello.py`
Why does Python throw a SyntaxError?
options: A. Because `hello.py` must be written in capital letters.
B. Because `python hello.py` is a system terminal command, not valid Python code to type inside the Python interpreter.
C. Because Python cannot run files from a hard drive.
D. Because the file must be named `main.py`.
items.explanation: This is one of the most common beginner traps: you run `python filename.py` in your operating system terminal, NOT inside the Python interactive shell (`>>>`).

items.prompt:
What will be printed to the screen when this script runs?
```python
print("Ready")
print("Set")
print("Go!")
```
options: A. Go! Set Ready
B. Ready Set Go! (all on one single line)
C. Ready\nSet\nGo! (each on a separate line)
D. Only Go!
items.explanation: Python executes code sequentially from top to bottom, and by default, each `print()` call displays its output on a new line.

items.explanation: Development starts in an editor, saves to disk as a `.py` file, and executes via the terminal.

items.explanation: The primary prompt for Python's interactive shell consists of three greater-than signs (`>>>`).

items.explanation: Python logical operators use short-circuit evaluation: `and` stops and returns the first falsy operand, while `or` stops and returns the first truthy operand without evaluating subsequent expressions.

items.title: Python is Case-Sensitive
items.content:
Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters as completely different things.

`print` is a valid built-in function.
`Print`, `PRINT`, or `PrInT` are not recognized and will cause a `NameError`.
items.explanation: Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters as completely different things. Mastering these rules prevents runtime errors and establishes robust programming foundations.

items.prompt: Fix the capitalization error in this line of code so it prints 'Welcome!':
items.explanation: Built-in functions in Python like `print()` must be written entirely in lowercase.
items.hint: Check the capitalization of the function name—Python uses lowercase for built-in functions like `print`.

items.prompt: Why are quotes required around the words inside `print("Hello")`?
options: A. Quotes indicate to Python that the contents are raw text (a string), rather than code commands or variable names.
B. Quotes make the computer whisper the output.
C. Quotes are only optional decorative characters.
D. Quotes tell Python to print to a physical printer.
items.explanation: Quotes delimit text data (strings). Without quotes, Python tries to interpret `Hello` as a variable or keyword.

items.prompt:
What is the difference between these two lines?
```python
print(2 + 2)
print("2 + 2")
```
options: A. Both lines output 4.
B. Both lines output '2 + 2'.
C. Line 1 outputs 4 (evaluates math), while Line 2 outputs '2 + 2' (literal text).
D. Line 2 causes a syntax error.
items.explanation: Unquoted numbers and math operators are computed by Python. Text wrapped in quotes is treated literally as characters.

items.prompt:
You type `python test.py` in your terminal and get this error:
`python: can't open file 'test.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory`
What is the most likely cause?
options: A. Python is not installed on your computer.
B. Your terminal is not currently in the same folder where `test.py` is saved, or the file was misspelled.
C. The Python code inside `test.py` has a syntax error.
D. You need an internet connection to run local files.
items.explanation: `No such file or directory` means Python looked in your current working directory and could not find a file with that name.

items.prompt: Does running a local Python script on your personal computer require an active Wi-Fi / internet connection?
options: A. Yes, Python must consult cloud servers to compile bytecode.
B. No, the Python interpreter runs entirely locally on your machine using your CPU and memory.
C. Yes, Python checks for software updates before every script execution.
D. Only on weekends.
items.explanation: Python is installed locally on your operating system. Once installed, executing scripts is 100% offline and local.

items.prompt:
Identify the syntax error in this Python 3 code:
```python
print "Hello"
```
options: A. The word `print` must be uppercase.
B. In Python 3, `print` is a function and requires parentheses: `print("Hello")`.
C. Strings cannot use double quotes.
D. Python requires a semicolon at the end of every line.
items.explanation: In Python 2, `print` was a statement. In Python 3, `print()` is a function and requires parentheses.

items.prompt: When saving a Python script, you should avoid spaces in the filename. Instead of `my program.py`, use an underscore: `my____.py`.
items.explanation: In Python variable names, letters, numbers, and the underscore `_` are the only legal characters. The underscore is the sole allowed special punctuation mark.

items.prompt:
What is the second line of output produced by this script?
```python
print("Step 1: Planning")
print("Step 2: Coding")
print("Step 3: Testing")
```
options: A. Step 1: Planning
B. Step 2: Coding
C. Step 3: Testing
D. None
items.explanation: The script prints sequentially. Line 1 prints 'Step 1: Planning', and line 2 prints 'Step 2: Coding'.

items.prompt: A student opens VS Code, types `print("Hello")`, but never saves the file or presses 'Run'. Why hasn't the text appeared on the screen?
options: A. VS Code is only a text editor used to write the instructions; it does not execute them until requested.
B. The code is running invisibly in the background.
C. Python only runs on computers that have a GPU.
D. The text was printed directly to a web browser.
items.explanation: Writing code in an editor simply prepares the text file. Execution requires sending that file to the Python interpreter.

items.prompt: You edit line 2 of your `game.py` script in your editor. You immediately switch to your terminal and rerun `python game.py`, but your changes don't appear. What did you forget to do?
options: A. Reinstall Python.
B. Save the file in your text editor (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S) before running it.
C. Restart the computer.
D. Rename the file to game2.py.
items.explanation: CPython reads the file stored on disk. If you haven't saved your changes in the editor, the file on disk still contains the old version.

items.prompt: You are building a program that will automate daily financial reports every morning at 8:00 AM. Which mode must you use?
items.explanation: Automated and production tasks always run from saved script files so they can be executed by system schedulers or other programs.
options: A. Run code interactively in the REPL one command at a time every day.
B. Write the logic in a .py script file and execute it using a task scheduler or CLI command.
C. Compile the Python script into a static BIOS firmware module.
D. Paste the Python source code into a word processor.

items.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes the complete lifecycle of running your first Python program?
items.explanation: This represents the full, correct programming cycle from code authoring to disk storage, interpreter invocation, and execution.
options: A. Write code -> Execute CPU instructions directly -> Output generated.
B. Write source code -> Save to .py file -> Python compiles to bytecode -> PVM executes bytecode -> Output generated.
C. Write code -> Run linker -> Create machine .exe -> OS executes binary.
D. Save file -> PVM parses text directly -> CPU generates machine code.
